claim: A vision-language-action manipulation policy can be made to recover on its own from two different kinds of trouble: arm poses that drift away from anything it was trained on while the scene itself is still workable, and failures that leave the scene in a state the task never passes through. The deciding bar is a strictly higher mean end-to-end task success rate than both the strongest earlier comparison system and the same policy without recovery training, together with a strictly higher success rate than that unmodified policy on every physical-robot task evaluated. Recovery has to happen without a human supplying correction during deployment, and has to leave the policy able to resume and finish the original task.

experiments: Build the policies the evaluation compares. Setup: for each simulation task, start from 10 human demonstrations and expand to 500 by a standard augmentation method. Inject perturbation-and-bridging segments at the start and between subtasks, up to 45 degrees of rotation and 0.5 m of translation, excluding the perturbation itself from the training targets so the policy learns only the recovery that follows. Separately, have a multimodal model watch failure videos to identify object-centric reset skills, collect 20 human demonstrations per skill and expand each to 500 the same way. Fine-tune separate task and reset adapters on a 3B-class policy with everything else frozen. At deployment an online monitor watches execution: pose drift gets no intervention, while a scene-breaking failure causes the matching reset adapter and prompt to be loaded, the reset executed, the task adapter reloaded once the scene is judged workable, and the task resumed.

End-to-end success across nine simulation tasks. Setup: nine tasks of varying difficulty, 50 trials each, against eight comparison systems including the same backbone policy without recovery training and a published recovery system in both autonomous and human-corrected forms. Result: the method averages 84.0% against 72.2% for the unmodified backbone, an 11.8-point gain, beating it on seven tasks and tying at 100% on one. The published recovery system averages 57.8% autonomously and 78.9% with human correction of its instructions, so the method beats the autonomous form but the human-corrected form remains the closest competitor. Remaining baselines average 38.0% to 48.0%.

Do the learned reset skills account for the gain on tasks whose failures break the scene? Setup: compare the full system, the same system without the reset stage, a reset-only variant, and a variant where a human rather than the model writes the reset instructions, on the four tasks where resettable failures occur. Result: the full system averages 73.5%; removing reset while keeping the perturbation training gives 70.0%, so reset is worth 3.5 points; reset alone gives 65.5%. The human-instruction variant reaches 80.5%, seven points above the full system, which marks how much of the remaining gap is the monitor's instruction quality rather than the recovery skills.

Does it hold on real hardware, without simulator state? Setup: run the unmodified backbone and the full system on a physical arm with two cameras for 40 trials each on a long-horizon stacking task and a contact-rich insertion task, with 10 human demonstrations expanded to 50 per task and per reset skill, using estimated object poses rather than ground-truth coordinates. Result: 62.5% to 75.0% on stacking and 45.0% to 55.0% on insertion, so the method beats the unmodified policy on both tasks, satisfying the every-task clause on the two tasks tested.
